title: How do you implement rate limiting in ASP.NET Core?
description: Built-in RateLimiter middleware, window strategies, partitioning, and what to return to clients.

data.text: **Question:** How do you implement rate limiting in ASP.NET Core?

ASP.NET Core ships built-in rate limiting middleware (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.RateLimiting`): you define named limiters (fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, concurrency) with a **partition function** per client, then apply them globally or per endpoint with `[EnableRateLimiting]`. Over-limit requests receive **429 Too Many Requests** with a `Retry-After` header. In distributed deployments, state must be shared (e.g. Redis-backed custom limiter) — the in-memory limiter counts per instance.

**Choosing a strategy:**
- **Fixed window** — simple counting per window; allows bursts at window edges (2× limit across a boundary)
- **Sliding window** — smooths the edge by rolling recent history; good default for APIs
- **Token bucket** — allows controlled bursts up to bucket size, then refills at a steady rate; ideal for public APIs
- **Concurrency limiter** — caps *in-flight* requests, protecting a slow dependency regardless of request rate

**Design points:**
- Partition by API key or user id when authenticated; fall back to remote IP for anonymous traffic
- Behind a proxy/CDN, use the forwarded header (`ForwardedHeaders` / `UseForwardedHeaders`) or you rate-limit the proxy itself
- Reject with 429 + `Retry-After` (seconds) so clients back off correctly; add `RateLimit` headers if useful
- Rate limits complement — not replace — authentication, and stop credential-stuffing/abuse on expensive endpoints
- Multi-instance apps: in-memory windows are per node; for global fairness use a shared store (Redis) or edge rate limiting (API gateway/CDN)

data.title: Sliding-window limiter with per-user partitions

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing which limiter fits which traffic shape (smooth vs bursty vs slow-dependency)
- Partitioning: per user/key vs per IP, and the proxy pitfall
- Correct client contract: 429 + Retry-After, idempotent retries
- Scale awareness: per-instance memory vs shared/global limiting

items: Limiting per IP behind a load balancer without forwarded headers — all users share one bucket
Choosing a fixed window and being surprised by double traffic at window boundaries
Blocking threads or queueing unboundedly while "waiting" for the slow endpoint
Returning 429 without Retry-After, so clients hammer faster
Applying rate limits only at the edge and leaving internal endpoints unlimited
Treating rate limiting as an anti-CSRF or anti-authentication control
Fixed window vs sliding window vs token bucket — which would you pick for a public API and why?
How do you keep rate-limit counters correct across 10 instances?
How does a concurrency limiter differ from a request-rate limiter?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Built-in middleware: fixed, sliding, token bucket, and concurrency limiters
Partition by API key/user (fall back to IP, honoring forwarded headers)
Respond 429 + Retry-After; keep health checks exempt
In-memory limits are per instance — distributed traffic needs shared state
data.takeaway: Pick the limiter that matches your traffic shape, partition per client, and remember: a per-node counter is not a global limit.
